children.value: We have been studying propositional logic which has allowed us to reason over a set of sentences which can each be evaluated as being True or False.

All computer scientists are logical
Alan is a computer scientist
Therefore Alan is logical
Each of these sentences is a proposition: they can all be evaluated as True of False. Can we prove this argument using propositional logic? Our arguments might be something like

If a person is a computer scientist then they are logical.
Alan is a computer scientist.
Therefore Alan is Logical.

Building and reasning over Knowledge Base with First Order Logic

children.label: Building and reasning over Knowledge Base with First Order Logic

children.value: What does this give us over what we can already do with propositional logic? Economy of representation and a clear structure. It will be helpful to develop a more extensive example to illustates this. Consider the following set of propositions:
P4: Alice is enrolled on the AI Course
P5: The AI Course require module ECS8050

Consider the question: does Diana advise (ie. teach) Alice? We can easily infer that she does by reading the sentences, but to determine this from a purely symbolic representation we would need an explicit rule that expresses this:
P1 \land P2 \land P3 \land P4 \land P5 \implies P6
children.html: P1∧P2∧P3∧P4∧P5  ⟹  P6P1 \land P2 \land P3 \land P4 \land P5 \implies P6P1∧P2∧P3∧P4∧P5⟹P6

children.value: where P6: “Diana advises Alice”. Given this rule, if all of P1-P5 are true, P6 must also be true (notice that we do not remove the possibility that there is another way in which Diana could advise Alice).
This does the job for this specific case, but
we would need a separate rule for every possible case
